questions.text: Although the senator was known for her ___ speeches, which often ran well past their allotted time, her written statements were models of brevity.
questions.explain: "Ran well past their allotted time" tells you the blank means long-winded, and "Although... brevity" confirms a contrast. Laconic is the opposite trap.

questions.text: The new manager's ___ approach, in which she consulted every employee before making even minor decisions, won her loyalty but slowed the department considerably.
questions.explain: The clause after the blank defines it: consulting everyone before deciding is a slow, deliberative style. High-handed is the opposite.

questions.text: Far from being ___, the scientist's conclusions were drawn only after years of painstaking experiments.
questions.explain: "Far from being" reverses what follows. The conclusions were painstaking, so the blank is the opposite: hasty. Rigorous describes what they were, not what they were far from.

questions.text: Critics who had expected the director's latest film to be as ___ as her earlier work were surprised by its restraint and quiet tone.
questions.explain: The critics were surprised by restraint, so they expected the opposite of restraint. Understated is the trap that matches the new film instead.

questions.text: The committee's report, though ___ in its details, was strikingly vague on the one question that mattered most: who would pay for the project.
questions.explain: "Though" sets up a contrast with "strikingly vague," so the details must be precise and careful.

questions.text: Despite his reputation as a ___ negotiator, the diplomat proved willing to compromise on nearly every point.
questions.explain: "Despite" plus "willing to compromise" means his reputation was for refusing to compromise. Tractable and pliant are a matching pair, but they mean the opposite.

questions.text: The professor's lectures were so ___ that even students with no background in the subject could follow them easily.
questions.explain: Easy to follow means clear. Engaging fits but has no partner, and abstruse and recondite are an opposite pair.

questions.text: The novel's plot is ___: characters appear and disappear without explanation, and events follow one another with no clear connection.
questions.explain: The colon explains the blank: no clear connection between events. Convoluted means twisted and complicated, not disconnected.

questions.text: Once considered a ___ figure in the town, the old judge had, by the end of his life, become a source of ridicule.
questions.explain: "Once... by the end... ridicule" signals a reversal, so he was once deeply respected.

questions.text: The early reviews were ___, but the play's audiences grew steadily as word of mouth spread.
questions.explain: "But audiences grew" contrasts with unenthusiastic reviews. Hostile fits alone; glowing and rapturous are a pair in the wrong direction.

questions.text: Because the evidence was largely ___, the jury was instructed not to give it the weight of direct testimony.
questions.explain: The contrast is with direct testimony. Circumstantial evidence is indirect, which is why it gets less weight.

questions.text: Her manner was so ___ that new colleagues often mistook her shyness for arrogance.
questions.explain: Shyness that looks like arrogance comes from holding back, so the manner is reserved. Gregarious and effusive go the other way.

questions.text: The company's growth was not the steady climb its founders had predicted but a ___ series of booms and collapses.
questions.explain: "Not the steady climb... but" requires the opposite of steady. Booms and collapses are erratic.

questions.text: Rather than ___ the opposition's arguments, the candidate chose to ignore them entirely, hoping voters would do the same.
questions.explain: "Rather than" contrasts with ignoring. The natural alternative to ignoring arguments is answering them. Overlook means the same as ignore.

questions.text: Even the critic's harshest reviews were ___ by a grudging admiration for the effort involved, so that artists rarely felt wholly dismissed.
questions.explain: Admiration that keeps artists from feeling dismissed softens the harshness. Tempered means moderated.

questions.text: The historian's account is ___, relying on a handful of letters to draw conclusions about an entire generation.
questions.explain: Large conclusions from little evidence means guesswork. Exhaustive and comprehensive are a pair in the opposite direction.

questions.text: Although the treaty was supposed to ___ tensions between the two nations, it seemed only to inflame them.
questions.explain: "Although... only to inflame" means the treaty was meant to reduce tension. Exacerbate and aggravate describe what actually happened.

questions.text: The young pianist's ___ was evident from the first notes: she played with a confidence and fluency that belied her age.
questions.explain: Confidence and fluency show great skill. Belied her age means her skill was beyond what her age suggested.

questions.text: Investors who had once been ___ about the startup's prospects grew wary after its third failed product launch.
questions.explain: "Once... grew wary" shows a change, so they were once hopeful.

questions.text: The governor's speech was full of ___, offering grand promises but few concrete proposals.
questions.explain: Grand promises with nothing concrete are empty, overused phrases.

questions.text: The biologist cautioned that the results were ___: a single study, however striking, could not establish a general rule.
questions.explain: The colon explains: one study cannot settle the question, so the results are tentative. Fraudulent is too extreme.

questions.text: Despite the general's reputation for ___, his memoirs reveal a man tormented by doubt about nearly every decision he made.
questions.explain: "Despite" contrasts the reputation with constant doubt, so the reputation was for decisiveness. Vacillation describes the memoirs instead.

questions.text: The author's prose is admirably ___; she never uses ten words where two will do.
questions.explain: The semicolon introduces an explanation: few words means economical.

questions.text: Because the tribe's customs had been recorded only by outsiders, anthropologists treated the existing accounts with considerable ___.
questions.explain: Outsiders' records may be unreliable, so careful scholars would doubt them.

questions.text: What began as a minor disagreement over procedure ___ into a bitter feud that divided the department for years.
questions.explain: Minor became bitter, so the conflict grew.

questions.text: Though the dancer's movements seemed ___, they were the product of years of rigorous training.
questions.explain: "Though... years of rigorous training" contrasts with movements that looked easy. Labored and strained are the opposite pair.

questions.text: The museum's new director, eager to ___ the institution's dusty image, filled its galleries with interactive exhibits.
questions.explain: She wants to get rid of the dusty image. Burnish means polish, which would improve an image, not remove it.

questions.text: Her colleagues found her ___ maddening: she would argue about the placement of a single comma for an hour.
questions.explain: Arguing over one comma shows excessive attention to small details.

questions.text: The once-thriving port had become ___, its warehouses empty and its trade dwindling year after year.
questions.explain: "Once-thriving" and empty warehouses signal decline. Flourishing and prosperous describe the past, not the present.

questions.text: Scientists were ___ by the fossil, which seemed to belong to no known species.
questions.explain: Something that fits no known category puzzles people. Delighted might fit, but it has no partner.

questions.text: The senator's ___ remarks, made off the record, caused a scandal when a reporter published them the next day.
questions.explain: Remarks that cause a scandal were unwise. Anodyne and judicious would not cause a scandal.

questions.text: Although the theory was initially ___ by most physicists, later experiments confirmed nearly all of its predictions.
questions.explain: "Although... later confirmed" contrasts with an initial negative reaction.

questions.text: The diplomat's ___ was legendary; she could deliver unwelcome news so gracefully that its recipients thanked her for it.
questions.explain: Delivering bad news gracefully is tact. Candor is honesty, but the sentence stresses grace, not frankness.

questions.text: The (i)___ of the evidence surprised investigators, who had expected the case to rest on a few ambiguous clues; instead, the documents were so (ii)___ that a conviction seemed certain.
questions.explain: They expected a few clues, so the surprise is a lot of evidence. A certain conviction needs strongly incriminating documents.

questions.text: Far from being (i)___, the reforms were the product of long deliberation, and their architects were (ii)___ about every detail.
questions.explain: "Far from being" reverses: the reforms were deliberate, so not impulsive. Careful architects were scrupulous about details.

questions.text: The essayist's reputation for (i)___ is undeserved: though her subjects are often weighty, she treats them with a (ii)___ that makes her work a pleasure to read.
questions.explain: The reputation is undeserved, and her work is a pleasure to read despite weighty subjects. So the reputation is for heaviness, and the reality is a light touch.

questions.text: The chief executive's ___ manner alienated employees, who felt that their suggestions were dismissed before they had finished speaking.
questions.explain: Cutting people off is abrupt and rude. Affable and genial are the opposite pair.

questions.text: Many readers find the philosopher's later works ___, filled with private terminology that he never bothers to define.
questions.explain: Undefined private terms make writing hard to understand.

questions.text: The candidate's ___ on the issue, supporting the plan one week and opposing it the next, cost him the trust of both camps.
questions.explain: Switching positions week to week is wavering. Consistency and intransigence go the other way.

questions.text: Though the documentary claims to be ___, it consistently presents only one side of the dispute.
questions.explain: "Though... only one side" contrasts with a claim of fairness.

questions.text: The ___ of the region's water supply became apparent only during the drought, when wells that had never failed ran dry within weeks.
questions.explain: Wells running dry quickly reveal how vulnerable the supply was.

questions.text: The editor praised the manuscript's ambition but found its argument ___, wandering from topic to topic without ever reaching a conclusion.
questions.explain: Wandering from topic to topic defines discursive. Cogent is the trap opposite.

questions.text: Rather than ___ the old building, the city chose to restore it, preserving its facade while modernizing its interior.
questions.explain: "Rather than" contrasts with restoring. The alternative to restoring is tearing down. Renovate is close to restore.

questions.text: The scientist's (i)___ in publishing her results was understandable: a premature announcement, if later (ii)___, would damage her credibility for years.
questions.explain: Avoiding a premature announcement is caution, and an announcement damages credibility only if it is later shown to be wrong.

questions.text: Though the painter was (i)___ during his lifetime, selling only a handful of works, his reputation has since (ii)___, and his canvases now command enormous prices.
questions.explain: Selling a handful of works shows he was little known, and enormous prices now show his reputation grew.

questions.text: The witness's testimony, at first (i)___, grew increasingly (ii)___ under cross-examination, as one detail after another proved impossible to reconcile with the evidence.
questions.explain: "At first... grew increasingly" shows a change. Details that fail to fit make the testimony doubtful, so it must have seemed believable at first.

questions.text: The professor's ___ comments, though brief, were invariably more useful than the lengthy reports her colleagues produced.
questions.explain: Brief but useful is concise and meaningful. Perfunctory is brief but careless, which conflicts with "more useful."

questions.text: Unlike his ___ predecessor, who rarely left his office, the new mayor seemed to be everywhere at once.
questions.explain: Rarely leaving the office describes someone who keeps to himself.

questions.text: The plan was ___ on paper, but it failed to account for the unpredictable behavior of the people it was meant to serve.
questions.explain: "But it failed" contrasts with a plan that looked workable on paper.

questions.text: The novelist's characters are so ___ that readers often forget they are fictional.
questions.explain: Forgetting characters are fictional means they seem real. Sympathetic fits loosely but has no partner.

questions.text: The economist's forecast, dismissed at the time as unduly ___, proved accurate when the market collapsed a year later.
questions.explain: A forecast that turned out right when the market collapsed was predicting bad news, so it was called too gloomy.

questions.text: Unlike the ___ prose of his early novels, which piled clause upon clause, the author's late style is spare to the point of austerity.
questions.explain: "Unlike" and "piled clause upon clause" point to elaborate prose, the opposite of spare.

questions.text: The new evidence did not ___ the older theory so much as refine it, clarifying the conditions under which it held.
questions.explain: "Did not X so much as refine" contrasts refining with a stronger action. Overturning is the strong alternative.

questions.text: Her (i)___ toward authority was well known; she had been (ii)___ from two schools before she was fifteen.
questions.explain: The second clause supports the first. Being thrown out of schools fits a defiant attitude.

questions.text: Because the ancient text survives only in (i)___ form, scholars must (ii)___ much of its content from quotations in later works.
questions.explain: If scholars rely on later quotations, the original is incomplete, so they must rebuild it.

questions.text: The committee's decision, though (i)___ in its reasoning, was (ii)___ in its effects: a careful argument led to a result that harmed precisely those it was meant to help.
questions.explain: The colon restates both blanks: careful argument, and a result opposite to its purpose.

questions.text: The general's ___ was so complete that he never once questioned the orders he received.
questions.explain: Never questioning orders is obedience.

questions.text: To the ___ eye, the two paintings appear identical; only an expert can spot the differences.
questions.explain: The contrast with "only an expert" means the blank describes a non-expert.

questions.text: The speaker's ___ remarks offended many in the audience, who had come expecting a serious discussion.
questions.explain: Expecting seriousness and getting offended means the remarks were not serious. Solemn and grave are the opposite pair.

questions.text: Although the city's population had ___ during the war, it recovered quickly once peace returned.
questions.explain: "Recovered" means the population had fallen.

questions.text: So ___ was the evidence against the defendant that even his own lawyer privately conceded the case was hopeless.
questions.explain: A hopeless defense means very strong evidence against the defendant.

questions.text: The philosopher was a born ___, delighting in arguments that overturned what everyone else took for granted.
questions.explain: Someone who attacks accepted beliefs is an iconoclast.

questions.text: Though she claimed to be ___ about the outcome, her constant checking of the results suggested otherwise.
questions.explain: Constant checking shows she cared, which contradicts a claim of not caring.

questions.text: The documentary (i)___ the complexities of the conflict, reducing a centuries-old dispute to a simple tale of heroes and villains; historians were (ii)___ by its distortions.
questions.explain: Reducing to a simple tale oversimplifies, and distortions would upset historians.

questions.text: The firm's (i)___ accounting practices, long tolerated by regulators, were finally exposed when an auditor refused to (ii)___ figures she knew to be false.
questions.explain: Practices that get exposed are questionable, and the auditor refused to approve false figures.

questions.text: Although (i)___ by nature, the senator could be remarkably (ii)___ when an issue she cared about came before the committee.
questions.explain: "Although" sets up a contrast: quiet by nature, but expressive when she cared.

questions.text: The tenor's voice, once powerful, had become ___ with age, barely carrying beyond the front rows.
questions.explain: Barely carrying means weak. Hoarse fits but has no partner.

questions.text: The study's conclusions are ___, since the sample of participants was too small to support any general claim.
questions.explain: Conclusions without adequate support are unjustified. Tentative is close, but it describes how a claim is offered, not whether it is supported.

questions.text: His apology seemed ___, delivered in a flat voice and followed immediately by a joke.
questions.explain: A flat voice and a quick joke suggest an apology made without real feeling.

questions.text: The region's climate is notoriously ___, with sunny mornings regularly giving way to violent afternoon storms.
questions.explain: Sudden changes mean unpredictable.

questions.text: The reviewer's praise was so ___ that readers suspected she was a friend of the author.
questions.explain: Praise extravagant enough to look suspicious is fulsome: excessive.

questions.text: Scientists once believed the deep ocean floor to be ___, but expeditions have revealed it to be teeming with life.
questions.explain: "But... teeming with life" contrasts with a belief that it was lifeless.

questions.text: The (i)___ of the new law is undeniable: it has already reduced pollution in the river. Its critics object not to its results but to its (ii)___, arguing that the regulations impose costs far greater than necessary.
questions.explain: Reducing pollution shows effectiveness. Costs far greater than necessary describe inefficiency, not the law's aims.

questions.text: Few historians have been as (i)___ as Lerner in acknowledging the limits of their evidence; where others offer confident conclusions, she offers (ii)___.
questions.explain: Openly acknowledging limits is candor, and the contrast with confident conclusions calls for hedged, limited claims.

questions.text: The novelist's early critics found her style (i)___, faulting it for an excess of ornament. Later readers, however, came to see that apparent (ii)___ as deliberate: each elaborate sentence, they argued, mirrored the (iii)___ of the social world she described.
questions.explain: An excess of ornament is baroque. "That apparent" refers back to the same excess. Elaborate sentences mirror a complicated world.

questions.text: Popular accounts tend to (i)___ the role of individual genius in scientific discovery, presenting breakthroughs as sudden flashes of insight. Historians of science, by contrast, emphasize the (ii)___ nature of most advances, which typically (iii)___ the slow accumulation of work by many hands.
questions.explain: Sudden flashes of insight overstate genius. "By contrast" calls for gradual progress, which relies on slow accumulation.

questions.text: The ambassador's remarks were deliberately ___, allowing both sides to read into them whatever they wished.
questions.explain: Remarks open to any reading are ambiguous. Forthright and candid are the opposite pair.

questions.text: Few could match the ___ of the old librarian, who seemed to have read every book in the collection.
questions.explain: Having read everything means deep knowledge. Curiosity fits loosely but has no partner.

questions.text: The new policy was intended to ___ abuses that had gone unchecked for decades.
questions.explain: "Gone unchecked" points to checking them now. Expose fits but has no partner.

questions.text: Even her admirers concede that the poet's later work is ___, recycling images and themes she had handled more freshly in her youth.
questions.explain: Recycled material handled less freshly is stale and overused.

questions.text: The mayor's response to the crisis was strikingly ___: she simply refused to acknowledge that anything was wrong.
questions.explain: Refusing to admit a problem is complacent: smugly unconcerned.

questions.text: Because the manuscript had passed through many hands, its ___ was in doubt; some scholars suspected it was a forgery produced centuries after the events it described.
questions.explain: Suspected forgery means its genuineness was doubted.

questions.text: Although the evidence for the theory is (i)___, consisting largely of a few suggestive observations, its proponents present it with a (ii)___ that would be appropriate only for a well-established fact.
questions.explain: A few observations is thin evidence. "Appropriate only for a well-established fact" means too much confidence.

questions.text: The CEO's (i)___ was matched only by her impatience; she could absorb a complicated report in minutes and had little tolerance for colleagues who (ii)___.
questions.explain: Absorbing reports in minutes shows sharpness, and impatience targets people who are slow.

questions.text: Despite its (i)___ beginnings in a rented garage, the company soon grew into a (ii)___ that dominated its industry. Its founders, however, remained curiously (iii)___, rarely granting interviews and avoiding the publicity their success might have brought.
questions.explain: A rented garage is a modest start, dominating an industry calls for an unstoppable force, and avoiding publicity is self-effacing.

questions.text: The critic's review was less a (i)___ of the novel than an attack on its author; rather than (ii)___ the book's arguments, it questioned the writer's motives, a tactic that readers rightly found (iii)___.
questions.explain: "Less an X than an attack" needs a neutral evaluation. "Rather than" contrasts with dealing with the arguments. "Rightly" signals readers disapproved.

questions.text: The professor's ___ manner made students reluctant to ask questions in class.
questions.explain: A manner that discourages questions is off-putting.

questions.text: What had seemed a ___ problem, easily solved by a minor adjustment, turned out to involve the design of the entire system.
questions.explain: "Seemed... turned out" contrasts the appearance with reality. It looked small and surface-level. Systemic describes what it turned out to be.

questions.text: The treaty negotiations, after months of ___, finally produced an agreement both sides could accept.
questions.explain: "After months of... finally" implies no progress before the breakthrough.

questions.text: A ___ observer of human behavior, the novelist could capture a character's essence in a single gesture.
questions.explain: Capturing essence in a gesture requires sharp insight.

questions.text: Her ___ in the face of criticism was striking: she neither defended herself nor seemed in the least disturbed.
questions.explain: Being undisturbed by criticism shows calm composure.

questions.text: The ___ of the evidence, which consisted of a single blurry photograph, did not stop the tabloids from declaring the creature's existence proven.
questions.explain: One blurry photo is weak evidence, and "did not stop" shows a contrast with the confident claim.

questions.text: The diplomat's (i)___ approach, which avoided public confrontation, was often mistaken for weakness; in fact, her quiet persistence (ii)___ concessions that louder colleagues had failed to win.
questions.explain: Avoiding confrontation is discreet, and "in fact" signals she succeeded in obtaining concessions.

questions.text: That the experiment failed is (i)___; what matters is that its failure (ii)___ a flaw in the theory that a success would have concealed.
questions.explain: "What matters is" contrasts with something unimportant. A failure that reveals what success would conceal exposes the flaw.

questions.text: The biographer's portrait of the composer is neither (i)___ nor hostile; she records his (ii)___ treatment of collaborators as candidly as she praises his music, and the result is a (iii)___ account that admirers and detractors alike have found convincing.
questions.explain: "Neither... nor hostile" needs the opposite extreme: worshipful. Recording faults candidly suggests poor treatment, and convincing both camps means balanced.

questions.text: In the decades after its publication, the treatise was (i)___, cited only by a handful of specialists. Its (ii)___ came only a century later, when economists recognized that it had (iii)___ ideas they had believed to be their own.
questions.explain: Cited only by a few means ignored. Later recognition is a rediscovery, and having the ideas first means it anticipated them.

questions.text: The commission's report ___ the agency for its slow response, calling its handling of the crisis inexcusable.
questions.explain: Calling something inexcusable is harsh criticism.

questions.text: Though the plan seemed ___ at first, its flaws soon became apparent.
questions.explain: "Though... flaws soon became apparent" contrasts with a good first impression.

questions.text: The tribe's way of life, long ___ by contact with the outside world, began to change rapidly once a road reached the valley.
questions.explain: Change began only once the road arrived, so before that the way of life was undisturbed.

questions.text: Critics ___ the film's special effects but found its story thin and its characters forgettable.
questions.explain: "But found its story thin" contrasts with praise for the effects.
